演奏時先在螺貝頂端附近開孔，再像吹號角般對孔吹氣；若裝有吹嘴則透過吹嘴發聲，若無: To play, a hole is first opened near the tip of the shell, and then you blow into the hole as if blowing a horn; if a mouthpiece is fitted the sound comes through the mouthpiece, and if not you blow straight into the hole. The pitch is adjusted by moving the hand in and out of the opening: the deeper the hand goes, the lower the note. Beginners can first practise blowing into the hole, then try changing the depth of the hand.

螺貝號作為氣鳴樂器，吹奏時以手在開口處進出調整音高。法國馬蘇拉斯洞穴出土的古代螺: As an aerophone the conch is played with the hand moving in and out of the opening to adjust the pitch. Ancient conches found in the Marsoulas cave in France have been blown again by researchers and a professional horn player. In India and Bangladesh, Bengali Hindu households blow a conch every evening as a ritual; in Aztec culture the conch was also used for ritual, war, music and festivals.

To play, a hole is usually opened near the top of the shell, with the aperture of the shell as the blowing end; some instruments have a separate mouthpiece and some do not. Known ancient specimens fixed a mouthpiece with organic material such as clay or wax. The source does not say what the remaining parts are made of.
螺貝號的音樂用途見於古代：1932年在法國庇里牛斯山馬蘇拉斯洞穴發現一件著名樂器: The conch's musical use is seen in ancient times: a famous instrument was found in 1932 in the Marsoulas cave in the French Pyrenees, and a CT scan showed that people had modified the shell to make a mouthpiece, fixed with clay or wax; researchers from the Sorbonne and a professional horn player blew it again. In the Americas it also appears among historical objects in the Larco Museum in Lima, Peru, and the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City. In Aztec culture the conch was used for ritual, war, art, music, myth, festival and the calendar.
螺貝號（Conch shell）屬H-S 423唇振氣鳴／號角與銅管，以中大型海: The conch shell belongs to H-S 423, lip-reed aerophones / horns and brass, and is made from a medium to large sea-snail shell. The player opens a hole near the top of the spire and blows as if blowing a horn, sometimes adding a mouthpiece; the depth of the hand in the opening adjusts the pitch, the deeper the lower. It is used in many places: ancient people modified conches to make instruments, Aztec culture used them for ritual, war, art, music, myth, festival and the calendar, and Bengali Hindus in India blow them every evening.
